title: What Does the Padlock in Your Browser Mean?
sources: Cloudflare Learning Center, 'Why is HTTP not secure? | HTTP vs. HTTPS' (cloudflare.com/learning/ssl/why-is-http-not-secure): HTTP requests and responses are sent in plaintext that anyone monitoring the connection can read; HTTPS uses TLS/SSL encryption to encrypt them
Cloudflare Learning Center, 'What is HTTPS?': HTTPS is HTTP with encryption (the S stands for secure); in the TLS handshake the browser and server agree on session keys used to encrypt the traffic

Chromium Blog / Help Net Security, 'Google Chrome will lose the lock icon for HTTPS-secured sites' (May 2023): Chrome 117 replaced the lock with a 'tune' icon; Google's 2021 research found only 11% of participants understood the lock's precise meaning; 'nearly all phishing sites use HTTPS, and therefore also display the lock icon'; the FBI warns the lock is not an indicator of website safety
Let's Encrypt (letsencrypt.org): a nonprofit certificate authority that gives out TLS certificates for free, so any site, including a scam site, can get the padlock

lines.text: What does the padlock in your browser actually mean?
it hops through strangers' machines on the way,
and with plain HTTP, it's like a postcard anyone can read.
But with HTTPS, the S means secure.
Your browser and the site agree on a secret key,
lines.caps: YOUR *BROWSER | AND THE *SITE | *AGREE ON | A *SECRET KEY

lines.text: that only the two of them can unlock.
That's what the padlock means: a private line.
But here's the twist: it doesn't mean the site is safe.
lines.caps: BUT *HERE'S | THE *TWIST | IT *DOESN'T | MEAN THE *SITE | IS *SAFE

lines.text: Nearly every scam site has a padlock too,
and since so few people knew what it meant,
Chrome swapped it for a different icon.
So the padlock locks the line, not the liar.
